topics.title: Combinators
topics.summary: Descendant, child, adjacent sibling and general sibling selectors describe relationships.
topics.description:
**Combinators** connect two selectors by their position in the HTML tree.

| Combinator | Syntax | Selects |
|---|---|---|
| Descendant | `A B` (space) | any B inside A, at any depth |
| Child | `A > B` | B that is a **direct** child of A |
| Adjacent sibling | `A + B` | the B immediately after A (same parent) |
| General sibling | `A ~ B` | every B after A (same parent) |
| Universal | `*` | every element (not a combinator but often grouped with them) |

### Examples in practice
```css
nav a            { }   /* every link inside nav */
ul > li          { }   /* only top-level items of that list */
h2 + p           { }   /* the paragraph right after each h2 */
input:checked ~ label { } /* labels after a checked input */
```

### Why child combinator matters
With nested lists, `ul li` also styles the nested items, but `ul > li` only styles the first level. The source course demonstrates this with brown (`.content-1 > ul > li`), pink (`p + li`) and purple (`p ~ li`) colors.

### Sibling combinators
They only look **forward** (later siblings), never backward. For "previous sibling" or "parent" logic use `:has()`.

### Specificity
Combinators add no specificity; only the simple selectors around them count.

### Tips
- Use `>` to avoid accidental deep matches.
- Lobotomized owl: `* + * { margin-top: 1em; }` adds spacing between all siblings except the first.
keyPoints: Space = any descendant; > = direct child
+ = next sibling only; ~ = all following siblings
Sibling combinators only look forward
Combinators add zero specificity
Use :has() when you need parent/previous-sibling logic
pitfalls: Using descendant selector and unintentionally styling deeply nested elements
Expecting + to match elements that are not adjacent

examples.title: Descendant vs child vs sibling
examples.css:
body { font-family: sans-serif; font-size: 18px; }
.menu li { color: green; }              /* all li, also nested */
.menu > li { font-weight: bold; }       /* only direct children */
.menu p + li { color: crimson; }        /* li right after a p */
.menu p ~ li { text-decoration: underline; } /* all li after a p */

examples.title: Lobotomized owl spacing
examples.css:
.stack > * + * { margin-top: 1rem; }
p { background: #e0f2fe; padding: 8px; margin: 0; font-family: sans-serif; }

interview.q: What is the difference between "div p" and "div > p"?
interview.a: "div p" matches every p inside a div at any depth; "div > p" matches only p elements that are direct children of the div.
+ selects only the immediately following sibling; ~ selects all following siblings that share the parent.

interview.q: Can CSS select a previous sibling or parent?
interview.a: Not with classic combinators, but :has() now makes it possible, e.g. li:has(+ li.active).

topics.title: Pseudo-classes
topics.summary: Style elements by state or position: :hover, :focus, :checked, :nth-child() and more.
topics.description:
A **pseudo-class** (single colon `:`) selects an element in a particular *state* or *position*.

### User-action states
- `:hover` pointer is over the element.
- `:active` being pressed.
- `:focus` has keyboard/mouse focus; `:focus-visible` only when the focus ring should show (keyboard).
- `:focus-within` the element or a descendant has focus.

### Form states
`:checked`, `:disabled`, `:enabled`, `:required`, `:optional`, `:valid`, `:invalid`, `:placeholder-shown`, `:read-only`.

### Structural (position)
| Selector | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `:first-child` / `:last-child` | first/last among all siblings |
| `:nth-child(n)` | n-th among all siblings |
| `:first-of-type` / `:last-of-type` | first/last of that tag among siblings |
| `:nth-of-type(n)` | n-th of that tag |
| `:only-child` | only child |
| `:empty` | has no children/text |

### nth-child formulas
- `:nth-child(odd)` / `:nth-child(even)`
- `:nth-child(3)` third item
- `:nth-child(3n)` every third
- `:nth-child(n+4)` from the fourth onward
- `:nth-child(-n+3)` only the first three
- `:nth-last-child(2)` counts from the end

### :first-child vs :first-of-type
`p:first-child` matches a paragraph only if it is the **very first child**. `p:first-of-type` matches the first paragraph even if a heading comes before it.

### Other useful ones
`:root` (html element, great for variables), `:target` (element whose id is in the URL hash), `:not()`, `:is()`, `:has()` (next topics).
keyPoints: Pseudo-class = state or position, single colon
:focus-visible shows focus rings only when appropriate
nth-child counts all siblings; nth-of-type counts same tag
nth-child(an+b) formulas: odd, even, 3n, n+4, -n+3
:root, :target, :checked are very handy
pitfalls: :first-child failing because another element comes first
Applying :hover effects without a touch/keyboard alternative
Using :nth-child(n) selectors that depend on fragile DOM order

topics.title: Pseudo-elements
topics.description:
A **pseudo-element** (double colon `::`) styles a *part* of an element or inserts virtual content.

### ::before and ::after
They create a virtual child **before/after** the element's content. They only render if `content` is set (even an empty string).

```css
.title::before { content: "★ "; color: gold; }
.title::after  { content: ""; display: block; width: 60%; border-bottom: 2px solid crimson; }
```

Typical uses: icons, decorative lines, badges, overlays, tooltips, clearfix, CSS shapes and loaders (see the Mini projects).

### Other pseudo-elements
| Pseudo-element | Targets |
|---|---|
| `::first-letter` | first letter (drop caps) |
| `::first-line` | first formatted line |
| `::selection` | highlighted text |
| `::marker` | list bullet/number |
| `::placeholder` | input placeholder text |
| `::backdrop` | behind <dialog>/fullscreen |
| `::file-selector-button` | file input button |

### Positioning trick
Make the parent `position: relative;` and the pseudo-element `position: absolute;` to place it precisely (underline animations, overlays, ribbons).

### Useful facts
- Pseudo-elements are not in the DOM; screen readers may read `content` text, so do not put essential content there.
- `content` accepts strings, `attr(data-label)`, counters and icons (font escape codes like `"\f121"`).
- Interactive effects: animate `::after` width on hover for an underline.
keyPoints: Use :: for pseudo-elements, : for pseudo-classes
::before/::after need the content property to render
Combine with position: relative/absolute for decorations
::first-letter, ::first-line, ::selection, ::marker style parts of text
Do not place essential content in pseudo-elements
pitfalls: Trying to add ::before to or (replaced elements)
Pseudo-element covering the element and blocking clicks (use pointer-events: none)

interview.q: Difference between a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element?
interview.a: A pseudo-class (:hover) selects an element in a state; a pseudo-element (::before) selects or creates a part of an element.
It has no content property. Add content: "" (or text) and, for shapes, give it display/size.

interview.q: Can you add ::before to an img?
interview.a: No - replaced elements have no content box for generated content; wrap the image or use a container.

topics.title: Modern Selectors: :is, :where, :not, :has
topics.summary: Functional pseudo-classes that shorten selectors and enable parent selection.
keyPoints: :is() shortens selector lists; takes highest specificity
:where() is the same but with zero specificity
:not() excludes; accepts a selector list
:has() selects parents / previous siblings based on content
:focus-within and :focus-visible improve form and keyboard UX
pitfalls: Not realising :is() raises specificity to its most specific argument
Using :has() with expensive broad selectors on huge DOMs

examples.title: :is() and :not()

interview.a: Both match any selector in a list. :is() contributes the specificity of its most specific argument; :where() contributes none, so it is easy to override.
It selects an element if it contains (or is followed by) elements matching the given selector - effectively a parent selector.

interview.q: How do you style a label when its checkbox is checked?
interview.a: If the input comes before the label: input:checked + label. Otherwise wrap and use .wrapper:has(input:checked) label.

topics.title: Native CSS Nesting
topics.summary: Write child rules inside parent rules with & - no preprocessor needed.
topics.description:
**CSS Nesting** lets you put one rule inside another, like Sass but built into the browser.

```css
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  background: white;

  & h2 { font-size: 1.5rem; }       /* .card h2 */
  & p + p { margin-top: .5rem; }

  &:hover { box-shadow: 0 4px 12px #0003; }  /* .card:hover */
  &.featured { border: 2px solid gold; }     /* .card.featured */
  &::after { content: ""; }                  /* .card::after */

  .dark & { background: #111; }              /* .dark .card */

  @media (width < 600px) {                   /* nested at-rules */
    padding: .5rem;
  }
}
```

### The & symbol
- `&` stands for the parent selector.
- It is **required** when you join without a space (`&:hover`, `&.active`) or place the parent later (`.dark &`).
- Modern browsers also allow nested type selectors without `&` (`h2 { }` inside `.card`), but using `&` is clearer and more compatible.

### Nested media/container queries
You can put `@media`, `@container`, `@supports` and `@layer` directly inside a rule, keeping the responsive code next to the component.

### Specificity
Nested selectors behave like `:is()` on the parent: the parent's most specific selector counts.

### Best practice
- Nest **2-3 levels** at most; deep nesting creates long selectors that are hard to override.
- Nest states (`&:hover`) and modifiers (`&.active`) - it is the biggest win.
- The source final project and float demo use this style (`& h1 { ... }`).
keyPoints: & represents the parent selector
Use &:hover, &.class, &::after for compound selectors
Media and container queries can be nested inside rules
Keep nesting shallow (2-3 levels)
No build step needed in modern browsers
pitfalls: Over-nesting that mirrors the HTML tree
Forgetting & when attaching a pseudo-class directly (":hover" alone means a descendant)
Using Sass-style &-suffix concatenation (.btn { &-primary {} }) - not supported natively

interview.q: What does & mean in native CSS nesting?
interview.a: It is the nesting selector that refers to the parent rule's selector, letting you write &:hover, &.active or .dark &.

interview.q: Do you still need Sass for nesting?
interview.a: Not for nesting - it is native now. Sass still offers mixins, loops, functions and &-suffix concatenation.
The nested rule is treated as if the parent were wrapped in :is(), so the parent's highest-specificity selector is used.
